H1.text: A closed bottle of water fogs up inside. A hot kiln turns chalky stone into lime and a gas.

H2.text: Solids, liquids and gases, all in one equilibrium. So which of them go into K?

H3.text: Diya covers a tumbler of water in her kitchen. Tiny drops gather under the lid.

H4.text: A full tumbler or a nearly empty one, the air above holds the same amount of vapour.

H5.text: By the end, you will know why some substances simply drop out of K.

P2.text: A phase is one even part of a mixture. One solid, one liquid, or one gas.

P3.text: Ice floating in water has two phases. Air is one phase, even with many gases in it.

P4.text: An equilibrium with more than one phase is called heterogeneous. Hetero means different.

S1.text: Let's put a closed jar of water on our molecule bench.

S2.text: Fast molecules escape from the surface into the air above. That is evaporation.

S3.text: Some vapour molecules hit the water and stick back. That is condensation.

S4.text: Soon both rates are equal. The vapour pressure stops changing.

S5.text: Now take out half the water. The vapour pressure stays exactly the same.

S6.text: So K here is just the pressure of the water vapour. K p equals p of water.

L1.text: Why does the liquid drop out? Think of a chocolate bar.

L2.text: Cut it in half. Each piece is smaller, but packed just as tightly.

L3.text: For a pure solid or a pure liquid, the packing is its concentration, moles per litre. It never changes, so we leave it out of K.

D1.text: Let's see it with the lime kiln, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. Solid calcium carbonate breaks into solid calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas.

D3.text: Step two. Write K the normal way. Calcium oxide times carbon dioxide, over calcium carbonate.

D4.text: Step three. Both solids have fixed concentrations. We fold them into the constant.

D5.text: Step four. K c equals the carbon dioxide concentration. And K p equals the pressure of carbon dioxide.

G2.text: Solid nickel and carbon monoxide gas make a nickel gas, used to purify nickel. The solid nickel drops out.

G3.text: Silver oxide with nitric acid. The solid and the liquid water drop out. Only the dissolved substances stay.

G4.text: Carbon dioxide with solid carbon gives carbon monoxide. Only the two gases stay.

G5.text: The rule. Keep gases and dissolved substances. Drop pure solids and pure liquids.

C1.text: Compare. A big lump of chalky stone and a small lump, in two closed boxes, at the same temperature.

K1.text: Pause and think. Which box ends with more carbon dioxide pressure?

K2.text: The same. The solid is not in K, so the gas pressure is fixed at that temperature.

R2.text: Some solid must stay in the box, even a tiny bit. If it is all used up, there is no equilibrium.

R3.text: NCERT gives a real value. At eleven hundred kelvin, the carbon dioxide pressure is two times ten to the five pascals.

R4.text: A pascal is a unit of pressure. Divide by one bar, which is ten to the five pascals.

R5.text: So K p equals two point zero zero, at that temperature only.

T1.text: Remember this. Pure solids and liquids stay out of K.

W2.text: Carbon dioxide plus carbon gives two carbon monoxide. K p is three point zero at a thousand kelvin. We start with zero point four eight bar of carbon dioxide and plenty of carbon.

W3.text: Let x bar of carbon dioxide react. It leaves zero point four eight minus x, and makes two x of carbon monoxide.

W4.text: K p equals two x squared over zero point four eight minus x. That equals three. Carbon stays out.

W5.text: Solve. Four x squared plus three x minus one point four four equals zero. So x is about zero point three three.

W6.text: Carbon monoxide is zero point six six bar. Carbon dioxide is zero point one five bar.

X2.text: Students put the solid into K, with calcium carbonate on the bottom.

X3.text: Leave it out. K p is just the pressure of carbon dioxide. Liquid water stays out too, but water vapour stays in.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Boards ask you to write K c or K p for a reaction with solids or liquids. Entrance tests ask for pressures from a total pressure.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Solid ammonium hydrogen sulphide is heated in a closed flask. It breaks into ammonia gas and hydrogen sulphide gas. At equilibrium the total pressure is zero point eight bar. Find K p. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Zero point one six bar squared.

A2.text: The solid stays out. K p equals the ammonia pressure times the hydrogen sulphide pressure.

A3.text: The two gases form one to one, so each is half the total. Zero point four bar.

A4.text: Zero point four times zero point four is zero point one six. A squared the total pressure.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is a pure solid left out of K?

Y3.text: Two. Write K p for calcium carbonate breaking down.

Y4.text: Three. Does adding more liquid water change its vapour pressure?

N1.text: Next time: K is huge for one reaction and tiny for another. What does that tell us? We find out in Applications of Equilibrium Constants.
